name: The AI Enablement Audit in Finance
title: The AI Enablement Audit in Finance
answer: The AI Enablement Audit in Finance is a structured review of how AI tools and models are introduced, used, and controlled across finance functions such as accounting, treasury, FP&A, credit, and financial reporting. It asks whether the organization has the right policies, data access, model documentation, and human oversight for each use case, from invoice coding to anomaly detection to forecasting. It also checks whether AI-enabled workflows are properly integrated with the general ledger, ERP, and reporting systems, and whether the audit trail is complete enough for internal and external review. The scope typically covers both third-party AI tools and internally built models, and it distinguishes between assistive tools that suggest and systems that act.

sections.body: The AI Enablement Audit in Finance is a structured review of how AI tools and models are introduced, used, and controlled across finance functions such as accounting, treasury, FP&A, credit, and financial reporting. It asks whether the organization has the right policies, data access, model documentation, and human oversight for each use case, from invoice coding to anomaly detection to forecasting. It also checks whether AI-enabled workflows are properly integrated with the general ledger, ERP, and reporting systems, and whether the audit trail is complete enough for internal and external review. The scope typically covers both third-party AI tools and internally built models, and it distinguishes between assistive tools that suggest and systems that act.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The audit runs on a mix of evidence sources and technical controls. On the technical side, it looks at identity and access management, data pipelines, cloud or on-premise compute, API connections, and logging and monitoring systems that record model inputs, outputs, and user actions. On the evidence side, it draws on policy documents, vendor contracts, model cards, validation reports, access reviews, and change logs. In finance, the infrastructure often spans ERP platforms, data warehouses, spreadsheets, and specialized AI tools, so the audit must trace data and decisions across those boundaries. It also considers how data is classified, encrypted, retained, and segregated between production and testing environments.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done through a combination of interviews, control testing, data walkthroughs, and sample-based review. Auditors map each AI use case to the finance process it supports, then test whether the stated controls, such as human review, threshold limits, and exception handling, actually operate. They inspect model documentation and validation evidence, check access rights against role definitions, and trace a sample of transactions or forecasts from source data to reported output. Where models are retrained or updated, the audit checks version control, approval records, and rollback plans. Findings are recorded with severity, root cause, and a management action plan, and the audit report is shared with the audit committee or equivalent body.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights, risk, and provenance are central to the audit. It examines who owns each AI system, who is accountable for its outputs, and what rights the organization has to the data and models it uses, including vendor licensing and third-party data terms. Provenance covers where training data came from, whether it is permitted for the intended use, and how lineage is documented from source to model to report. Risk assessment covers model error, bias, privacy, security, and operational dependency, and it links to the organization's broader compliance obligations. The site tracks 219 compliance and regulation pages and 148 active AI lawsuits, which illustrate the volume of external expectations and disputes that can shape an audit's scope, and the audit also checks whether incident response, model decommissioning, and vendor exit plans are in place.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The AI Enablement Audit is moving from a periodic, checklist exercise toward continuous monitoring and embedded controls. As finance teams adopt more generative and agentic tools, audits are likely to focus more on real-time logging, model behavior drift, and the boundary between human and automated decisions. Regulators and standard setters are adding expectations for documentation, testing, and accountability, and the site's 219 compliance and regulation pages reflect that growing body of guidance. The audit will also need to keep pace with the 732 AI tools tracked on the site, since tool sprawl increases the risk of unmanaged data flows and shadow AI. Over time, the audit may become a standing capability that feeds risk dashboards and board reporting rather than a once-a-year review.
